running HarloOs on my Bitaxe gamma 601 , how do you know when you have
overclocked it too far on MHZ , how do you see the chip erros ?
Searched the web · Bitaxe Gamma hardware errors AsicJobs counter overclock too
Searched the web · Harlo OS firmware harlolabs download release notes
Searched the web · esp-miner web UI hardware errors errorPercentage expected ha

Hi there, happy to go through this.

Short version first: on a Gamma 601 the frequency number is not what tells you if you went too far. Two things tell you, and they are both in the miner's own interface: the hardware error rate, and your measured hashrate compared to the expected hashrate for the settings you chose.

The error figure comes straight off the chip. The B.1370 keeps a cumulative error counter in register 0x4C, and the firmware reads it and turns it into the "hashrate error %" you see on single chip Bitaxe devices.
That stat is computed as error count over total count
, so it is
error hashrate over valid hashrate
. In the web interface it sits on the dashboard next to hashrate and efficiency. If you prefer raw numbers, open http://your-miner-ip/api/system/info in a browser and look at errorPercentage, hashRate and expectedHashrate in the JSON. That JSON is the most honest view you can get without a serial cable.

How to read it while tuning: at a healthy setting the error percentage sits low and flat and the measured hashrate tracks expectedHashrate closely. When you push past what the chip will do at that core voltage, you get one of two patterns. Either the error percentage starts climbing and stays up, which means the chip is returning bad hashes and you are burning watts for nothing, or the hashrate quietly falls short of expected even though errors look fine. That second pattern is the sneaky one.
One owner tuning a BM1370 found the measured hashrate sitting about 1.5 to 2 percent below the theoretical expected value, and only raising core voltage brought it back in line, which means the chip had been discarding or miscomputing work at the margin without that showing up anywhere obvious.
 So treat any persistent gap between hashRate and expectedHashrate as a failed overclock, even with a clean error number.

Two things that will fool you if nobody warns you. First,
the error figure reads high for the first measurement window after boot, and that is real ASIC error during the frequency ramp up rather than a glitch
, so ignore the first few minutes after any change. Second, on the 601 a whole hash domain can go silent and the error percentage will not flag it at all, because
errorPercentage is error hashrate divided by current hashrate, so a silent domain does not raise it
.
In one reported case a domain sat at 0 GH/s for five days, the device kept mining at about 75 percent of expectedHashrate, and errorPercentage stayed at 0.
 If your JSON has a hashrateMonitor section, check the per domain figures there, and if one is at or near zero, a restart usually brings it back. Worth knowing too that on this chip
a domain dropping out around 690 MHz on an otherwise healthy build looks like that particular chip's own overclock limit
, and every chip binning is slightly different, so your ceiling is yours alone.

The method I would use: change one thing at a time, frequency or voltage, never both, in steps of about 10 to 25 MHz. After each step let it settle at least thirty minutes, then compare three numbers, the error percentage, measured versus expected hashrate, and the accepted hashrate your pool reports over a few hours. The pool number is the only one that pays, and it lags, so give it time. Back off one step from the first setting where errors climb, hashrate falls short, or the unit reboots on its own. Keep an eye on temperature the whole time, because
the Gamma draws more power than earlier revisions and is much easier to overheat, especially on the stock heatsink and fan
, and a hot chip will throw errors that look like an unstable clock when the real problem is cooling.

One housekeeping note before you tune anything: check which Harlo OS version you are on, in the System section of the web interface, against the current one at harlolabs.com, and update first if you are behind. BM1370 behaviour has genuinely changed between firmware builds, so chasing a stability problem on an old build wastes your evening. If you are already on Harlo OS, take the OTA image rather than the factory one, since the OTA keeps your wifi, pools and theme.

If you want to compare notes with people running the same board at the edge, the Harlo Discord is at https://discord.gg/Q2R5sA9Fsf and JD, our hardware lead, is @nullhashrate there. Send me your current frequency, core voltage, error percentage and ASIC temperature and I will tell you how much headroom I think you have.

Thanks for the good question, and happy tuning.
Hal, HeliumDeploy Technical Support

Hey, quick question about the pool. I’m mining on Harlo and rooting for
that next block, so I wanted to check something since a lot of rented hash
came on.

From the outside everything looks healthy: the API is fast, jobs are on the
current BCH tip, and shares are being accepted. But there hasn’t been a
block since #····,809 on Oct 27, and the best share has been stuck at 334.6G
since at least Nov 2, even with the pool showing 14–17 PH/s. It could just
be bad luck, but I’d like to rule out a problem.

Could you check a few things on your side?

Are stale or rejected share rates normal since the rented hash came on,
especially from the rental connections?
Is every share checked against the full network target, including shares
from high-difficulty rental connections? In other words, would a
block-winning share from a rental definitely be submitted to the node?
Does the displayed hashrate match the accepted share difficulty over time,
or could it be overstated?
Does the best share figure reset after each block, or is it all-time?
Thanks for all your work on this. Not complaining, just want to make sure
nothing’s being missed.
Searched the web · Bitcoin Cash network hashrate EH/s November 2026
Handed to the team · Pool server-side data (reject/stale logs, share validation path, best-share rese

Hey, this is a good set of questions and I would rather be asked them than not.

Let me separate what I can answer from what needs someone with the pool backend in front of them, because the four things you asked are not all the same kind of question.

The general mechanics first. On a stratum pool every share that arrives is rehashed by the server and compared against two targets, the share difficulty assigned to that connection and the full network target. The share difficulty only decides whether it counts toward your accounting and your paid work. The network target check happens on the same hash. That means a block winning share cannot be filtered out by a high share difficulty, because by definition it is far above any share difficulty the pool would ever set. A rental connection at, say, 500K share difficulty submits fewer shares, not less valid ones, and any one of them that happens to be under the network target is still under the network target when the pool checks it. The failure modes that genuinely do lose blocks are different: a job that is stale because the pool was slow to push a new BCH tip, or a node submission that errors and is not retried. Your observation that jobs are on the current tip and the API is fast argues against the first one.

On displayed hashrate, a pool number is always an estimate derived from accepted share difficulty over a rolling window. It is not measured. So it can read high in exactly one honest way, which is lag: rented hash that connects and disconnects in bursts leaves the window averaging over work that is no longer there. Over a few days of steady rental that effect washes out, so a sustained 14 to 17 PH/s reading should be broadly real if the share accounting behind it is sound.

Now the part that caught my eye, and it is the best share, not the block drought. The drought itself is unremarkable, a pool at a few PH/s against the BCH network can easily go a week or more between blocks and that is just the geometry of it. But best share is a much tighter statistic. The expected best share over a period is roughly total hashes divided by 2^32. At 15 PH/s over the nine days since Oct 27 that is about 1.2 times 10 to the 22 hashes, which puts the expected best share in the low single digit trillions, call it 2 to 3T. You are seeing 334.6G, frozen since Nov 2. That is close to an order of magnitude below what that much hash should have thrown off by chance, and a frozen best share with real hash arriving is the specific shape you would see if the high difficulty rental connections are being counted toward the hashrate display but their shares are not being run through the best share comparison. That would be a display and accounting issue rather than a lost block, since the network target check sits on a different code path, but it is worth proving rather than assuming.

What I cannot do is read our pool's logs, the reject and stale counters per connection, the node submission path, or whether best share in our implementation is all time or resets at each block. I will not guess at our own code. I have handed the whole thing to JD, who runs the pool and firmware side, with your numbers and the arithmetic above. He is back on at 10am Eastern today and the answer comes to you right here in this thread.

If you want it faster, he is in our Discord at https://discord.gg/Q2R5sA9Fsf as @nullhashrate and he is usually quicker to a question there than to anything else.

Thanks for raising it properly instead of just grumbling about luck.
Hal, HeliumDeploy Technical Support

Handed to the team · Roadmap question on firmware support for non-ESP32 industrial Antminers; I will

Hey, short honest answer: not today, and the reason is architectural rather than a matter of someone getting round to it.

Harlo OS is built for ESP32-S3 based miners. The whole thing, the flasher profiles, the ASIC drivers, the display engine, assumes a microcontroller talking to one or a handful of BM13xx chips over a serial link, with the web interface served straight off that same chip. That is the Bitaxe, NerdQaxe, NerdOctaxe, Hammer, Thor P2 and Jingle class of machine, and the current supported list plus what is coming is kept up to date at https://harlolabs.com/.

An S21 or an S19k Pro is a different animal. Those run a full Linux control board driving three hashboards with dozens of chips each, with their own PSU control, chain detection and fan logic. Porting to that is not adding a hardware profile, it is a second firmware project, which is why that space belongs to Braiins OS and the Vnish type builds rather than to anything ESP32 based. You are already on Braiins on your S21 and honestly that is the right tool for it.

Whether an Antminer class port is anywhere on the plan is JD's call, not mine, and I am not going to invent an answer for you. I have put it to him along with the Thor X1 question you asked and the pool audit, and he is on today, so his answer comes back to you in this thread. If you would rather get him talking directly, he is @nullhashrate in our Discord at https://discord.gg/Q2R5sA9Fsf and roadmap chat is exactly what that channel is for.

For what it is worth, your S21 on Braiins at 16.6 J/TH is not a machine that needs rescuing by different firmware.
